# The Efficient Market Hypothesis and random walks

This assignment compares a forecasting strategy built on the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH)
against the two non-trivial models you have met: simple exponential smoothing, and exponential
smoothing with an additive damped trend.

The EMH says that in a perfectly efficient market, prices are accurate and already reflect all
available information. If that holds, no amount of analysis lets you beat the market consistently.

In his 1970 paper ([1]), Eugene Fama set out three forms of the hypothesis, differing in what counts
as available information:

1. *Weak form*: the information in past prices.
2. *Semi-strong form*: all public information, past prices included.
3. *Strong form*: private information as well.

This assignment takes the weak form and uses nothing but past prices. Stated in the language of this
course, the weak form says that a price series is a random walk: the value at time t is the value at
t-1 plus an uncorrelated white-noise shock.

$$
y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t
$$

So the change from one day to the next is pure noise.

$$
y_t - y_{t-1} =  \varepsilon_t
$$

That is the Naive method. The Naive forecast at time T+h, beyond the training data, is the last
observed value:

$$
\hat{y}_{T+h|T} = y_T
$$

Set h=1 and substitute t=T+1, as in the session on benchmark models, and you get the fitted values of
the Naive model:

$$
\hat{y}_{t|t-1} = y_{t-1} \ \ \ \ \ \text{(fitted values of the Naive model)}
$$

Residuals are the series minus the fitted values, so for the Naive model:

$$
y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1} = y_t - y_{t-1}
$$

If the series really is a random walk, those residuals are uncorrelated white noise. The random walk
equation says the same thing:

$$
y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \rightarrow y_t - y_{t-1} = \varepsilon_t
$$

So the question this assignment answers is a concrete one. **Can either exponential smoothing model
beat the Naive method on a stock index?** If neither can, the weak form of the EMH survives the test.
Question 8 also tests the random walk directly, on the residuals of the Naive model.

The data is the daily closing level of the **Euro Stoxx 50**, the blue-chip index of the euro area,
from October 2023 to June 2026.

### **2. Build two training sets, holding 80% and 60% of the data** (0 points)

Complete the code below. The result is a single tsibble in which `.id` identifies the training set.

NOTE: `stretch_tsibble()` is not used here, because we want exactly two training sets.

```{r}
n_obs_80 <- # Your code goes here. The whole number of observations closest to 80% of the data
n_obs_60 <- # Your code goes here. The whole number of observations closest to 60% of the data
n_obs_list <- c(n_obs_60, n_obs_80)
train_sets <- tibble() # EMPTY TIBBLE THE DATA IS INSERTED INTO

# The loop builds the training sets and stacks them into one dataframe.
# Just run it.
for (i in seq_along(n_obs_list)) {
  train_i <- tr_data |> slice(1:n_obs_list[i]) |> mutate(.id = i)
  train_sets <- bind_rows(train_sets, train_i)
}

# Turn it back into a tsibble so the fable library accepts it.
# Just run it.
train_sets <- as_tsibble(train_sets, key = .id, index = trading_day)
```
